english.html: ily believed and assured that the prisoner was Martin Guerre their brother,

notes.citation: A Latin hexameter on death — source not identified
notes.original: Illa malis requiem finemq́; laboribus affert.
notes.gloss: Perhaps a humanist line or Coras's own; it is not Virgil, Ovid, Horace or Seneca in this form.

english.html: Women have this peculiar to them, says the Philosopher, that they believe lightly, and are easy to be deceived by the ruses and wiles of men <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>.

notes.citation: Aristotle, History of Animals IX, at the opening (IX.1, 608b: the female is "more easily deceived", εὐαπατητότερον); the print's de natura auiũ, "of the nature of birds", is a wrong sort or slip for animalium
notes.original: Ariſtote au cõmencement du ix. liu. de natura auiũ.
notes.gloss: Book IX opens with the characters of the two sexes: the female softer, more jealous, more querulous, more shameless, more false of speech, more easily deceived and of better memory.

english.html: Such, to be sure, was the nature of the men of old: to deceive the female kind, those credulous hearts <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>.

notes.citation: Publio Fausto Andrelini (Faustus, of Forlì, c. 1462–1518), Livia (the Amores), book IV
notes.gloss: The couplet: Scilicet ista fuit veterum natura virorum, / fallere femineum, credula corda, genus. Andrelini's Livia, an elegiac collection in four books (Paris, 1490), was a school text in France in Coras's youth; the line and its place in book IV are unverified.

english.html: And the Emperor Justinian said: we have sufficiently known the feeble nature of women, subject to a thousand trickeries and circumventions <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>.

notes.citation: Novels (the Authenticum), collation 7, the title De aequalitate dotis et propter nuptias donationis (Nov. 97), at the paragraph Quaesitum (chapter unverified)
notes.original: P. quæſitũ. de æqua dor. aux nouuelles ſous la collation vij.
notes.gloss: De æqua dor. = De aequalitate dotis; the P. is the print's sort for §. Justinian's legislation on the dowry repeatedly pleads the weakness of women and their exposure to deception as its ground.

english.html: Joined to the incredible longing which the same de Rols had to recover her husband: things which persuaded her too easily that the prisoner was he, especially as he gave several private and particular tokens; but from the moment she began to perceive the fraud, she wished a hundred thousand times for death, which she would have executed upon herself but for the fear of God.
Although death is the end of all evils, the rest from all misery, and a strong bulwark against the calamities of this world —
It brings to our ills rest, and to our labours an end (Illa malis requiem finemque laboribus affert).

And although for that reason it ought not to be dreaded by a man of worth, but rather contemned and despised <sup class="mk" data-key="a2">a2</sup>; and although Numantius, writing to Marcus Cicero, says that one ought often to desire an honest death, by which a man passes beyond innumerable perils and crosses of the inconstant fortune of this miserable world — so far is it from being a thing one ought

notes.citation: Cicero, Letters to his Friends (Epistulae ad familiares), books V and VI — the consolatory letters of 46–45 BC (to Titius, Fam. 5.16; to Torquatus, 6.3–4; to Toranius, 6.21), where death is said to be no evil and even to be wished for in such times
notes.original: Ciceron au v. & vj. liure de ſes epiſt.
